2.6. Spatial motion analysis
393
Translation and rotation data were determined during each of
394
the three scans and analyzed separately. The maximum transla-
395
tion and rotation from one acquisition to the next across the entire
396
time series and across all three scans was compared to speciﬁc cri-
397
teria (translations to one half the size of the voxel size or 0.75 mm
398
and rotations to 1.5◦) via a one-sample t-test. Furthermore, two-
399
way RM ANOVA was utilized to compare the maximum, mean,
400
and the variability of translational and rotational motion across
401
axis and scan condition. For these analyses realignment parameters
402
were transformed by taking the absolute value of the difference
403
from one acquisition to the next and therefore represent abso-
404
lute motion across acquisitions. Graphical presentation of all data
405
depicts mean ± SEM, and any points without error bars indicate
406
instances in which the SEM is encompassed by the data. All graph-
407
ical data presentations were created using GraphPad Prism 4 (La
408
Jolla, CA), all statistical tests were performed using SigmaStat 3 (San
409
Jose, CA), and signiﬁcance was arbitrated at a p < 0.05.
410
2.6.1. fMRI data analysis
411
Analyses
were
carried
out
using
the
standard
image
412
analysis
package
Statistical
Parametric
Mapping
version
5
413
(SPM5—Wellcome
Trust
Center
for
Neuroimaging,
London,
414
UK) supplemented by custom software written in the matrix
415
based programming environments IDL (ITT, Boulder, CO) and
416
MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA). Preprocessing of the images
417
was initiated via placement of both the anatomical and func-
418
tional images in AC-PC alignment and in gross registration to
419
one another. Time series realignment using a 6 parameter rigid
420
body algorithm (Cox and Jesmanowicz, 1999; Woods et al., 1993)
421
to reduce the inﬂuence of any subject motion was then carried
422
out. Concurrently, ﬁeld inhomogeneity data were used to correct
423
any geometric distortions in the EPI images using an automated
424
algorithm that takes into account the interaction between motion
425
and inhomogeneities and has been shown to result in an improved
426
coregistration between EPI and T1 images (Cox and Jesmanowicz,
427
1999; Hutton et al., 2002). Anatomical data were then segmented
428
into gray matter, white matter, and bias corrected images. Func-
429
tional data were then spatially normalized to the bias corrected
430
(intensity normalized) anatomical images and spatially smoothed
431
using a kernel with a full width at half max equal to two times
432
the native resolution of the image (i.e. 3 mm). Linear drift was
433
accounted for by global normalization across the time series and
434
high-pass ﬁltering. Whole brain analysis was carried out on a pixel
435
by pixel basis using a parametric general linear statistical model.
436
This analysis was conﬁned to gray matter pixels using a custom
437
generated mask to exclude any white matter or ventricle pixels
438
that was applied to the data prior to statistical analysis. Motion
439
parameters were used as covariates within this model to remove
440
the inﬂuence of subject motion on the subsequent results. The
441
general linear model ﬁt was based on a ﬂexible boxcar design using
442
the canonical hemodynamic response function and corrections
443
for multiple comparisons were carried out such the probability
444
of a type I error was maintained at 5% (Genovese et al., 2002).
445
Finally, the timecourse of the MR signal was determined in the
446
voxel that showed the local maximum correlation to presentation
447
of the visual stimulus (in visual cortex) or administration of
448
cocaine (in the anterior cingulate). The signal measured under
449
each condition was averaged across all three subjects. Graphical
450
data presentations were created using GraphPad Prism 4 (La Jolla,
451
CA).
452
3. Results
453
Under the conditions employed, rhesus monkeys could be reli-
454
ably acclimated to undergo fMRI scans while awake. The integrity
455
of the imaging data necessitated that subjects were minimally
456
stressed and near motionless. To objectively assess the effective-
457
ness of the training procedure in minimizing any stress to the
458
subject, physiological and endocrine measurements were taken, in
459
fully acclimated subjects, over 2 h sessions in either the custom
460
fMRI apparatus or in a standard primate chair (with the exception
461
of the respiratory rate data—see Section 2). In each condition, phys-
462
iological measurements were taken over three sessions whereas
463
endocrine measurements were taken over two sessions. In the
464
custom fMRI cradle, one-way RM ANOVA reveal no main effect
465
of heart rate (F2,2 = 0.295; p = 0.760), respiratory rate (F2,2 = 2.027;
466
p = 0.212), blood pressure (F2,2 = 0.051; p = 0.951), and tempera-
467
ture (F2,2 = 5.528; p = 0.096) as a function of session. The powers
468
of these tests were 0.051, 0.155, 0.051, and 0.214, respectively.
469
In the primate chair (or custom apparatus without head restraint
470
for respiratory rate data), heart rate (F2,2 = 2.537; p = 0.194), res-
471
piratory rate (F2,2 = 2.501; p = 0.125), blood pressure (F2,2 = 2.154;
472
p = 0.213), and temperature (F2,2 = 0.967; p = 0.454) were not sig-
473
niﬁcantly different as a function of session. The powers of these
474
tests were 0.177, 0.586, 0.158, and 0.051, respectively. Data from
475
each session were then averaged. A two-way RM ANOVA was
476
then used to determine if there were signiﬁcant differences as a
477
function of the apparatus used or the time spent in a given appara-
478
tus. Heart rate (F2,1 = 0.074; p = 0.811), respiratory rate (F2,1 = 0.342;
479
p = 0.618), blood pressure (F2,1 = 1.875; p = 0.304), rectal tempera-
480
ture (F2,1 = 0.002; p = 0.968), and plasma cortisol levels (F2,1 = 1.854;
481
p = 0.306) did not signiﬁcantly differ by condition. The powers of
482
these tests were 0.058, 0.085, 0.096, 0.058, and 0.095, respec-
483
tively. Furthermore, there was no main effect of time spent in the
484
apparatus for heart rate (F2,3 = 0.395; p = 0.762), respiratory rate
485
(F2,3 = 3.156; p = 0.107), blood pressure (F2,3 = 1.152; p = 0.402), rec-
486
tal temperature (F2,3 = 0.402; p = 0.757), or plasma cortisol levels
487
(F2,4 = 2.230; p = 0.155). The powers of these tests were 0.050, 0.636,
488
0.066, 0.051, and 0.234, respectively. Mean basal plasma cortisol
489
levels were, prior to research personnel entering the colony, were
490
22.925 ± 2.764 and 26.313 ± 4.202 g/dl on the days when mea-
491
surements were subsequently collected in the custom cradle or the
492
commercial chair, respectively. Analysis via a paired t-test revealed
493
that basal plasma cortisol levels did not differ across these different
494
days (t3 = −3.388; p = 0.148). The power of this test was 0.230.
495
In addition to a stable physiology, good quality fMRI data
496
requires minimal subject motion. Fig. 4 shows transformed realign-
497
ment parameters across the three translational and rotational axes,
498
assuming rigid body motion, averaged across the three subjects.
499

500
mum, mean, and standard deviation of the motion from acquisition
501

502
lational and rotational movements were signiﬁcantly less (p < 0.05)
503

504

506

509
